final_message:
All five versions are written, and every one matches the expected output byte-for-byte on the three samples and on 60 random cases I generated. The benchmark-size outputs also agree across all five.

**Algorithm (all versions):** the standard DP from SPEC.md, one row of 64-bit costs updated in place, with the diagonal and left values held in locals. Each pair's insertion costs and letter codes are computed once up front. Input is read whole and parsed as bytes or tokens, without per-pair string allocation.

**Speed choices by language:**
- **C++:** `fread` the whole file and build the output in one string. Stdout is set to binary so line endings are `\n`, matching the expected files. The min is ordered so only one compare sits on the loop-carried chain (138 ms vs 211 ms before). I also tried a prefix-minimum reformulation; it wasn't faster, so I reverted it.
- **Java:** the input is parsed straight from the byte array, no `String` tokens. The DP is a static method so the JIT compiles it early, and scratch arrays are reused. Java is about 2–3× slower than C++ on the DP, and JVM startup adds about 220 ms.
- **C#:** pinned pointers in the hot loop, so no bounds checks. `Math.Min` compiled to unpredictable branches, so I used a branch-free min (1093 ms → 416 ms). In `solution.csproj` I turned on `TieredCompilationQuickJitForLoops=false` (so the hot method is fully optimized from the start), turned off concurrent GC, and enabled `UseSystemResourceKeys`. No package references.
- **Go:** substitution rows are `[256]int64` indexed by a `uint8` letter code, which removes the bounds check on the hot lookup. Slices are reused and output is written once.
- **JavaScript:** typed arrays for the row and costs. When the file is about 2 MB or less, costs fit in int32 and the min is branch-free, which halved the time (1410 ms → 707 ms). Larger inputs use a Float64Array path with ternary mins; I checked it gives the same output as the int32 path on the benchmark.

**Results:**
- C++: passes s1, s2, s3 and all random cases.
- Java: passes s1, s2, s3 and all random cases.
- C#: passes s1, s2, s3 and all random cases.
- Go: passes s1, s2, s3 and all random cases.
- JavaScript: passes s1, s2, s3 and all random cases.

Benchmark-size input (300 pairs, about 90M cells), best of three runs, machine shared with other load, so treat these as rough: C++ 134–233 ms, Go 202–230 ms, C# 386–416 ms, Java 423–524 ms, JavaScript 600–660 ms. I did not measure memory use.

**Test tooling (in `tools/`):** `reference.py` is a literal pure-Python implementation of the recurrence, `gen.py` makes random inputs, and `run_all.py` runs every program against samples and random cases with exact comparison and times the benchmark input. `tools/cases/` holds the 60 random cases, their expected outputs and `bench.in`; delete it if you don't want it.

**Not done:** I did not try SIMD or anti-diagonal vectorization, which would be the next step for C++. I also did not check whether the Go and Java built-in mins compile to branches, which the C# result suggests they might; a branch-free min could help both. I did not test CRLF input files, though all parsers treat any byte ≤ 0x20 as whitespace.

request.prompt:
You are writing five versions of the same program, in C++, Java, C#, Go and JavaScript, for a comparison of
how fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Each language has its own folder with a starting file and a `build.cmd`. The benchmark builds every program with
these same build scripts and flags, whatever you change in them. Write these programs:

1. `cpp/main.cpp` (more `.cpp` and header files in `cpp/` are fine): C++20, built by `cpp\build.cmd` with
   Microsoft Visual C++ 19.40 (Visual Studio 2022) and `/O2 /GL /EHsc /std:c++20`. Standard library only, plus
   nlohmann/json 3.12 (`#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>`, already in `cpp/include/`). Run as
   `cpp\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
2. `java/src/Main.java` (more `.java` files in `java/src/` are fine): Java 23, built by `java\build.cmd` with
   `javac`. Java SE only, plus Jackson 2.22 (core, databind and annotations, already in `java/lib/`). Run as
   `java\run.cmd INPUT_PATH`, which runs `java -cp "out;lib\*" Main` with the default JVM settings.
3. `csharp/Program.cs` (more `.cs` files in `csharp/` are fine): C# 12 on .NET 8, built in Release by
   `csharp\build.cmd`. Base class library only. You may change properties in `csharp/solution.csproj`, but do not
   add package references. Run as `csharp\out\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
4. `go/main.go` (more `.go` files in `go/` are fine): Go 1.27, built by `go\build.cmd`. Standard library only.
   Run as `go\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
5. `js/main.js`: JavaScript on Node.js 22, with no build step. Built-in Node modules only; no npm packages. Run as
   `node js\main.js INPUT_PATH`.

Each program reads the input file whose path is its first argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments) and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input. Python 3.13 (`C:\Python313\python.exe`) is
available if you want it for testing, but not as part of any program.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Build and test all five versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside
this folder, and take at most about 60 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time: never stop
a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example `taskkill /IM java.exe` or
`Stop-Process -Name node`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
